title: As My Career Lay Dying

jokes.text: Larry announces his retirement on air, crowd goes 'Aww,' and he immediately pivots: 'I will see you, uh, tomorrow night.'
jokes.setup: Larry gives a heartfelt, seemingly final announcement that he will not be coming back when his contract ends.
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts the gravitas by saying he'll see them tomorrow night — the pathos deflated in an instant.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical moment: the 'Aww' from the audience sets up a sentimental beat, then Larry's flat pivot to 'see you tomorrow night' deflates all the drama he just manufactured. It's pure Larry Sanders — he courts pathos and then retreats from it immediately. Character-specific and structurally tight.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Banana liqueur. I needed a drink a couple of hours ago. This was the only thing I could find.

jokes.text: 'No flipping.' — Larry's sign-off catchphrase delivered after the retirement announcement.
jokes.setup: Larry has just made a major emotional announcement about leaving the show.
jokes.punchline: He ends with his rote commercial-break catchphrase 'No flipping,' which is absurdly mundane given the gravitas of what just happened.
jokes.explanation: The catchphrase is a running gag across the series, but here it lands with particular irony — after announcing he's quitting, Larry still reflexively tells the audience not to flip channels. The contrast between the enormity of the news and the triviality of the habit is perfectly Larry. High economy: two words, big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: My breath smells like a monkey's asshole.

jokes.text: 'This is... mmm. Banana liqueur. I needed a drink a couple of hours ago. This was the only thing I could find.'
jokes.setup: Someone catches Hank still at the studio in the middle of the night holding a mysterious bottle
jokes.punchline: It's banana liqueur — the saddest, most undignified possible choice of drink for a man having an existential crisis
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'banana liqueur' is the joke — it's not whiskey or gin, it's the most pathetic, novelty-shelf liquor imaginable. Perfectly chosen to humiliate Hank's dignity while he's trying to perform gravitas about the show ending. The pause before naming it ('this is... mmm') sells the embarrassment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: There's a fire extinguisher there. It has a simple elegance, and yet it has strength.

jokes.text: 'My breath smells like a monkey's asshole.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been drinking banana liqueur all night because it was the only thing he could find.
jokes.punchline: His self-assessment of the consequences is delivered with complete, resigned matter-of-factness.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'monkey's asshole' is the key — banana liqueur logically leads there, and Hank delivers it with the weary self-awareness of a man who has made many poor decisions. Highly quotable, perfect economy, and completely in character for Tambor's sad-sack grandeur.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: I thought when Larry announced his retirement from the show, I would wake up, because I have that nightmare almost every night.

jokes.text: Hank waxes rhapsodic about a fire extinguisher: 'It has a simple elegance, and yet it has strength.'
jokes.setup: Hank says he has spent all night in the studio and never really looked around closely.
jokes.punchline: What he has discovered and is moved by is a fire extinguisher, which he describes with the reverence of a man encountering fine art.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully absurd character moment. Hank's alcoholic all-nighter has brought him to a state of banana-liqueur enlightenment where a fire extinguisher becomes profound. The deadpan description ('simple elegance... and yet it has strength') is delightful and very specific to Hank's pompous self-delusion. High originality for the visual object chosen.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Hard.

jokes.text: Hank confesses he has the nightmare of Larry announcing his retirement 'almost every night' and thought he would wake up.
jokes.setup: Hank explains his disbelief that Larry is actually leaving.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that this nightmare recurs almost every night — his deepest fear is losing his meal ticket — is darkly funny and pathetically on-brand.
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the pathology: Hank's subconscious has been screaming at him about his co-dependency on Larry for years. 'Almost every night' is the killer qualifier — it transforms a one-time fear into a chronic existential dread. Very Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Jim Gray
dialogue.line: I think the ratings were even higher for the super bowl than they were for the 3rd rock episode. A very special 3rd rock.

jokes.text: Hank asks to be pinched to see if he's dreaming, then escalates: 'Harder. Hard.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks Brian to pinch him to confirm this is real.
jokes.punchline: He keeps asking for it harder, in a beat that goes from comedic to vaguely uncomfortable — Hank channeling his anguish into physical sensation.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'pinch me' to 'harder' to 'hard' is a reliable comedic structure — the joke is in Hank's need to feel something real. Not original but well-executed in the moment with Tambor's physicality implied.

dialogue.line: Right in between Richard Simmons and jenny mccarthy.

jokes.text: During the on-air show, Larry notices a red mark on Hank's face and Hank claims it's 'an allergy' — but the audience has just seen Hank getting pinched repeatedly.
jokes.setup: Larry, on-camera, notices a red mark on Hank's face and asks about it.
jokes.punchline: Hank deadpans 'I have an allergy' — but the viewer knows it's from the pinching sequence.
jokes.explanation: A classic Larry Sanders structural joke — the behind-the-scenes chaos bleeds into the on-air segment. The audience is ahead of Larry, which makes Hank's straight-faced 'allergy' explanation a perfect deadpan lie. Excellent structure: the callback rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Bob Costas
dialogue.line: Everyone knows you're the reason we lost football.

jokes.text: The on-air segment with Bob Costas and Jim Gray completely falls apart as Hank, Larry, and apparently someone else are all having separate phone conversations about a ranch, the Super Bowl, and Jay Leno appearances simultaneously.
jokes.setup: A live on-air interview segment with sports journalists Bob Costas and Jim Gray is supposed to be a focused conversation.
jokes.punchline: The segment devolves into overlapping, disconnected conversations — someone discussing buying ranch land with a spring creek, someone talking about a Jay Leno appearance sandwiched between Richard Simmons and Jenny McCarthy — all while the interview is nominally happening.
jokes.explanation: The chaos of the segment is funny in the way Larry Sanders often is — professional TV falling apart in real time. The specificity of 'right in between Richard Simmons and Jenny McCarthy' grounds the absurdism. Slightly hard to parse from transcript alone.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you want to sit there and stare like a moron and breathe though your mouth, you can go sit in jenny jones' audience.

jokes.text: 'How many acres?' — Larry's completely disconnected question mid-interview, apparently responding to a private sidebar conversation about a ranch
jokes.setup: Bob Costas is in the middle of discussing something; background chatter about a ranch has been bleeding in
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'how many acres?' reveals he has completely lost the interview thread and is now participating in the real-estate side conversation
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly capture Larry's distraction and the show's entropy. Economy is the chief virtue here — the non sequitur does a lot of heavy lifting about how chaotic this taping has become.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You better climb back on board and towel off, because we're gonna finish the show in a blaze of glory.

jokes.text: Artie tears into Hank backstage: 'You think you're gonna jump off the sinking ship? Well, I got news for you, rat boy. You better climb back on board and towel off, because we're gonna finish the show in a blaze of glory.'
jokes.setup: Artie confronts Hank about his checked-out, mopey behavior during the broadcast.
jokes.punchline: 'Rat boy' and 'towel off' are the absurd peaks of an escalating dressing-down — Artie's motivational speech is so aggressive it becomes its own kind of comedy.
jokes.explanation: This is pure Artie — the manager who expresses love through volcanic fury. 'Rat boy' is a perfectly absurd insult, and 'towel off' is unexpected enough after 'climb back on board' that it gets a real laugh. Rip Torn's character could only deliver this. High character integration score because no other character on television talks like this.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Just like when you hit on Michael landon's wife. He was dead. That woman was sitting shivah.

jokes.text: 'If you want to sit there and stare like a moron and breathe through your mouth, you can go sit in Jenny Jones' audience.'
jokes.setup: Artie continues his furious dressing-down of Hank.
jokes.punchline: The specific threat of exile to the Jenny Jones audience — daytime talk show trash-TV — as the ultimate degradation is a perfectly calibrated industry-insider insult.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity of Jenny Jones — not just 'daytime TV' but the particular brand of lowest-rung tabloid fare — makes this an insider joke that also works as pure character comedy. The escalating physicality ('breathe through your mouth') before the punchline is textbook structure. Only Artie could say this, and only on this show.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You put your tongue in her mouth.

dialogue.speaker: Brian
dialogue.line: I lost my balance. I was falling over, and I stuck my tongue out to break my fall.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Someone who can reach the top shelf.'
jokes.setup: Beverly asks what qualities Artie is looking for in a new assistant.
jokes.punchline: Artie's answer is completely literal and dismissive — height as the only qualification — implying Beverly is too short and the conversation is over.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy: five words that accomplish multiple things simultaneously — dismisses Beverly, makes a physical joke at her expense, and reveals Artie's contempt for the whole conversation. It's the kind of line that gets quoted from the show. Could only come from this character in this moment. Justified 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Pure comedy Gold. Melt it, mint it, and ship it to fort knox.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Jesus Christ. The body's not even dead yet. You're already making your move, aren't ya? Just like when you hit on Michael Landon's wife.'
jokes.setup: Beverly has shamelessly angled for the job. Artie calls her out.
jokes.punchline: Artie escalates by comparing her opportunism to hitting on a widow — and specifically Michael Landon's wife, which makes it specific, celebrity-grounded, and darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: The Michael Landon reference is a sharp industry-insider joke — Landon was a beloved TV figure, which makes hitting on his recently widowed wife a particularly vivid image of shamelessness. The specificity elevates what could have been a generic accusation.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Pussy-whipped. Flying right back to St. Louis.

jokes.text: Hank defends himself: 'He was dead. That woman was sitting shivah. I was consoling her.' — then adds: 'I lost my balance. I was falling over, and I stuck my tongue out to break my fall.'
jokes.setup: Artie accuses Hank of putting his tongue in Michael Landon's widow's mouth while she was sitting shivah.
jokes.punchline: Hank's defense — that he 'lost his balance' and 'stuck his tongue out to break my fall' — is an absurdly committed rationalization delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The setup is already funny (hitting on a widow at shivah), but Hank's defense reaches a level of delusional self-justification that is both jaw-dropping and perfectly character-true. 'I stuck my tongue out to break my fall' is an extraordinary piece of writing — physically absurd, deeply revealing of Hank's psychology, and delivered with Tambor's signature wounded sincerity. 'Why doesn't anybody understand this?' makes it a complete comedic thought. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy anchor example — shocking escalation, perfect character integration, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Fred de Cordova
dialogue.line: Very talented... basketball player.

jokes.text: Fred de Cordova described as Artie's 'old drinking compadre' — casual throwaway revealing Artie's network of legendary industry veterans
jokes.setup: Artie declines lunch, citing plans with Fred de Cordova (Johnny Carson's longtime Tonight Show producer)
jokes.punchline: The word 'compadre' plus the casualness of name-dropping a Tonight Show legend as a drinking buddy is pure Artie characterization
jokes.explanation: Insider comedy for people who know the Tonight Show history. Works as texture and character-building but doesn't land as a standalone joke for general audiences.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Your boyfriend was over? Ignoring that.

jokes.text: Fred de Cordova advises Hank: 'My advice is to take any job you can get.' — Hank's potential employers: Roseanne, Donny and Marie, and Magic Johnson.
jokes.setup: Artie/Fred is lunching with Hank, who insists he's getting plenty of calls.
jokes.punchline: His list — Roseanne, Donny and Marie, Magic Johnson — is a descending spiral of desperation, each one a more alarming option than the last. Magic Johnson's inclusion as a TV employer gets the kicker: 'Very talented... basketball player.'
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of 'very talented / very talented / very talented... basketball player' is a classic comedy-of-threes with a devastating button. The pause before 'basketball player' is where the laugh lives. Good structure, well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: I saw my face reflected in the, uh, in the cooktop, and I said... 'lemons.'

jokes.text: Beverly admits she has a meeting with Leno — then reveals she told everyone she was going to the doctor.
jokes.setup: Beverly has been going on about not wanting anyone to think she's going behind Larry's back.
jokes.punchline: She immediately reveals she lied to everyone, including the people she just told she wasn't going behind Larry's back — blind to her own hypocrisy.
jokes.explanation: A nice self-incriminating moment — Beverly's complete lack of self-awareness is her defining comic trait. The structure is solid: she condemns the behavior, then immediately demonstrates it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: lemons. When life gives you lemons, you make things with lemons.

jokes.text: Larry says he was on his way to the kitchen 'for a stiff one' — someone replies 'Your boyfriend was over?'
jokes.setup: Larry is sharing his emotional journey from last night, building to a meaningful moment of self-reflection.
jokes.punchline: The sexual double entendre on 'stiff one' is jumped on immediately with 'Your boyfriend was over?' — a sharp, quick deflation of Larry's gravitas.
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient, and funny as a puncturing device. The gay joke is dated but the structure — interrupting Larry's self-important monologue — is well-executed. 'Ignoring that' is a perfect reaction, which slightly elevates the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Little... little playlets, really.

jokes.text: Larry's moment of revelation, staring at his reflection in the cooktop: 'Lemons. When life gives you lemons, you make things with lemons.'
jokes.setup: Larry is building toward a meaningful personal epiphany.
jokes.punchline: He delivers the most watered-down version of the 'when life gives you lemons' cliché imaginable — 'you make things with lemons' — then concludes he can go back to his acting career.
jokes.explanation: The garbled cliché — 'you make things with lemons' instead of lemonade — is funny on its own, but the pivot to 'I can go back to my acting career' (which we know is a delusion) turns the moment into a layered Larry Sanders joke about self-deception dressed up as self-actualization.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: She stepped on every one of my fucking lines.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Oh, I know. I saw that production. And you said you enjoyed it, right?

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: That's what I said.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Hank, I wasn't aware that you ever had an acting career.'
jokes.setup: Hank announces he will return to his acting career.
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat, direct, completely sincere statement that he wasn't aware Hank had one.
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's deadpan is the delivery vehicle — the comedy is in how Artie doesn't soften it at all. Perfect economy, clean structure.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Move along, chinaman.

jokes.text: Hank's acting credits: cruise ship shows, a production of Love Letters with Ruth Buzzi in Thousand Oaks ('Little playlets, really'), and one episode of Kung Fu.
jokes.setup: Hank is defending the existence of his acting career.
jokes.punchline: His credits descend in prestige — from cruise ships to community theater with Ruth Buzzi to a single episode of Kung Fu. Each one is more dispiriting than the last.
jokes.explanation: The list works as a comedic descent. 'Little playlets, really' is a perfect self-conscious qualifier — Hank knows they're not great even as he's citing them. Ruth Buzzi as a scene partner lands as its own joke for anyone who knows her career.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I hate to be the one to rain on your parade, but doing a play with Ruth buzzi and saying, 'move along, chinaman,' do not an acting career make.

jokes.text: Hank: 'She stepped on every one of my fucking lines.' Then someone admits they saw that production and said they enjoyed it — 'Yeah. That's what I said. And I did.'
jokes.setup: Hank complains about Ruth Buzzi stepping on his lines in Love Letters.
jokes.punchline: Someone (Artie) admits to having seen the production and claimed to enjoy it — then immediately clarifies: 'Yeah. That's what I said.' The implication that he lied is left hanging.
jokes.explanation: The polite lie exposed — 'That's what I said' vs. 'And I did' — is a small but neat comedy beat. The ambiguity ('And I did' could be sincere or could be doubling down on the lie) is the interesting part.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Well, there's no shame in doing porno.

jokes.text: Hank's one TV acting credit: an episode of Kung Fu in which he played a merchant. His line: 'Move along, chinaman.'
jokes.setup: Hank reveals his one television acting credit.
jokes.punchline: 'Move along, chinaman' — delivered with pride, then repeated, then explained in detail ('he's standing in front of my store... and he kicked my ass').
jokes.explanation: The joke operates on multiple levels: the line itself is racist and clueless, Hank is proud of it, and then he explains the plot with complete earnestness ('he kicked my ass. He was a nice guy'). The kicker — 'He was one of the Carradine brothers' — grounds it in Hollywood lore and adds another layer. Dark and character-true.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Hey, now. We barely know each other.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I hate to be the one to rain on your parade, but doing a play with Ruth Buzzi and saying "Move along, chinaman" do not an acting career make.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just laid out his full acting résumé.
jokes.punchline: Artie summarizes it in one devastating sentence — naming the two most embarrassing elements and delivering the verdict flatly.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect callback and summary joke. Artie picks out exactly the two most absurd data points, inverted syntax ('do not an acting career make') gives it a Yoda-esque formality that elevates it above a plain insult, and the delivery would be bone-dry. High economy, excellent structure. Justified 8+ score — comparable to the 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' anchor in its perfectly calibrated dismissiveness.

dialogue.line: He cannot act.
I know.
Don't worry.
Don't worry.

jokes.text: Hank fires back that he called his agent and has an acting gig — Artie responds: 'Well, there's no shame in doing porno.'
jokes.setup: Hank triumphantly announces his agent has already gotten him an acting gig.
jokes.punchline: Before Hank can reveal what it is, Artie preempts with 'Well, there's no shame in doing porno' — which is actually the funniest possible assumption given everything we've just heard.
jokes.explanation: Timing is everything here. Artie's preemptive guess — delivered before Hank can speak — is the correct comedic move. Given Hank's résumé (just established), porno is a logical next step. The deadpan 'no shame in it' framing is perfectly Artie. Good callback energy to the résumé discussion without being a formal callback.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: I think they're gonna want to hear the 'hey, now' when they see me.

jokes.text: The actual gig: 'Caroline in the City.'
jokes.setup: Artie has guessed 'porno.' The real answer is built up.
jokes.punchline: Caroline in the City — a real but decidedly mid-tier NBC sitcom — lands as almost as bad as porno in this context.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on industry-insider recognition — Caroline in the City is real and was genuinely considered a second-tier show, so Hank's pride in landing it is itself funny. The show's credibility as a punching bag is necessary for the joke to land fully.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And now I have to sit next to that... that... that... that woman.

jokes.text: Hank arrives on the Caroline in the City set and immediately begins saying 'Hey, now' unprompted during the run-through.
jokes.setup: Hank is supposed to play a plumber in a scripted scene. He has lines.
jokes.punchline: He keeps inserting his trademark catchphrase 'Hey, now' into scenes where it does not belong, as if he cannot separate himself from his on-air persona.
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliant piece of character comedy — Hank cannot act because he cannot stop being Hank. The 'Hey, now' intrusions into the plumber scene expose that Hank has no real self outside his on-air persona. The joke also comments on the nature of celebrity vanity and stunt casting. High character integration because this joke is entirely specific to this character and this show.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Jesus, Sidney, will you please get up, and will you help me here?

jokes.text: The Caroline in the City producer says 'I don't think there are any "hey, nows" in there' — gently pointing out what the entire room already knows.
jokes.setup: Hank has just 'Hey, nowed' through the entire scene.
jokes.punchline: The producer's massively understated observation that the script does not contain any 'Hey, nows' is the cringe comedy peak.
jokes.explanation: Pure understatement as comedy. The restraint of 'I don't think there are any Hey, Nows in there' when the correct response would be to throw Hank out is the Larry Sanders Show at its finest — people being professionally polite in the face of catastrophic behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: So... what, did you hire a black man?

jokes.text: The producer goes backstage and says: 'He cannot act. I know. Don't worry. Just tell him not to say Hey, now.'
jokes.setup: The producer has just witnessed Hank's disastrous run-through.
jokes.punchline: His crisis management is not 'get rid of him' but 'just tell him not to say Hey, now' — as if that's the only problem with Hank's performance.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the minimalism of the solution — fix one symptom while ignoring the terminal condition. A Hollywood production-politics joke that works because it's true.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Well, you said you went a different way. I mean, how many different ways are there?

jokes.text: Hank explains his reasoning: 'I think they're gonna want to hear the "hey, now" when they see me. I mean, I'm just tellin' ya.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just said 'Hey, now' when explicitly told not to.
jokes.punchline: He not only defends it but believes it's what they secretly want — the delusion is complete.
jokes.explanation: Hank's self-delusion reaches full flower here. His logic — 'they'll want it when they see me' — is both the funniest possible rationalization and a precise character statement: Hank has never been able to separate his persona from his person.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: By things... by things, he means crying, by the way.

jokes.text: 'Why don't we take five, everybody.' — the director calls a break after Hank's second 'Hey, now.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just explained why he had to say 'Hey, now' again.
jokes.punchline: The production simply surrenders: 'Why don't we take five, everybody.' Said with the weariness of a man who has accepted defeat.
jokes.explanation: The resignation in calling a five-minute break as an alternative to continuing to deal with Hank is a good reaction beat. Not big on its own but it punctuates the sequence well.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: for those of you who are watching tonight, the unemployment line starts right to the right of pat.

jokes.text: Hank on the phone: 'I'll tell you what the problem is. It's Lea and her little slave master Fred Barron. They're bad-mouthing me — going around telling people I can't act. What do you mean how do I know? I know. Because they said it to me, OK?'
jokes.setup: Hank calls his agent to complain that people are saying he can't act.
jokes.punchline: His evidence that they're secretly bad-mouthing him is that they told him directly to his face — which means it's not behind his back at all.
jokes.explanation: A classic Hank self-incrimination loop: he's upset people are bad-mouthing him, but his proof is that they said it to him directly. The logic collapse is funny and also a perfect window into Hank's paranoid solipsism. The 'Because they said it to me, OK?' kicker is the best line.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: For those of you who are watching tonight, the unemployment line starts right to the right of pat.

jokes.text: Larry, on air with a guest, is so distracted he randomly pivots: 'Why don't we come back, and we'll talk about your earrings when we come back from the commercial break. Would you like to do that? Because that's our jewelry segment.'
jokes.setup: Larry is conducting an interview but is clearly mentally elsewhere — distracted by the show's impending end.
jokes.punchline: He invents a 'jewelry segment' on the fly to cover his distraction, offering to discuss earrings as if this is a normal show pivot.
jokes.explanation: Larry's professional autopilot kicking in to cover for his personal crisis is funny and character-true. 'That's our jewelry segment' — as if this is an established thing — is the absurdist note that elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Pat Sajak
dialogue.line: the state of liberty. Uh, Hank? Merv? Pat. And, Hank, it's 'statue.' Statue of liberty.

jokes.text: Artie's reaction (implied) after walking someone out, then a new candidate appears. Artie says flatly: 'We just, uh... we just went a different way.'
jokes.setup: Someone — apparently a job candidate — has just been rejected.
jokes.punchline: 'We just went a different way' — the Hollywood passive-voice rejection delivered with zero affect — is followed by an implied awkward pause.
jokes.explanation: The industry-specific joke about Hollywood non-answers is clean and well-executed. 'We went a different way' is a real phrase used to fire/reject people, so Artie deploying it is both funny and industry-savvy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? Jeff. My name's Jeff. You called me Jim.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: I called... I'm sorry. Who's this fucking guy?

jokes.text: The new candidate's response to 'We went a different way': 'So... what, did you hire a black man?'
jokes.setup: Artie gives the standard Hollywood rejection brush-off.
jokes.punchline: The candidate immediately jumps to a specific, race-based interpretation of 'different way' — and then doubles down: 'I mean, how many different ways are there?'
jokes.explanation: Unexpected and specific enough to be genuinely surprising. The joke subverts the genteel Hollywood-speak of 'we went a different way' by stripping it to its possible racial-hiring subtext. 'How many different ways are there?' is the comedy engine — the implication that there are only a few 'ways' you can go is darkly funny and industry-truthful. High originality.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: The correct title is the new colossus, so I guess you should worry a little less about your name and a little more about these, uh... these questions.

jokes.text: Larry is interviewing Pat Sajak about Wheel of Fortune. Sajak explains there are international versions with local hosts: 'So there are pat and vannas all over the world.' Larry: 'A frightening thought.'
jokes.setup: Pat Sajak explains that Wheel of Fortune is franchised internationally with local hosts.
jokes.punchline: Larry's reaction — 'A frightening thought' — about the existence of multiple Pat Sajaks across the globe is a perfectly dry aside.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-aimed poke — Sajak playing along with Larry gently mocking the Wheel of Fortune brand. The subtext (that Sajak himself is somewhat of a bland cultural product, hence the 'frightening' proliferation) makes it sharper than it appears.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Well, not to worry, debbie, with a body like yours, you don't have to be smart.

jokes.text: Hank interrupts the Pat Sajak interview to volunteer himself for Sajak's new game show, citing his credential: 'Hank has hosted the Chabad telethon.'
jokes.setup: Sajak is discussing his new game show and mentions they're looking for a host.
jokes.punchline: Hank volunteers himself using the Chabad telethon as his primary hosting credential — pitching himself in front of Sajak and, presumably, the live audience.
jokes.explanation: Hank self-promoting on Larry's own show, in front of a guest, using the Chabad telethon as a credential, is exactly the kind of oblivious desperation that defines Hank Kingsley. The Chabad specificity is the joke — it's the Jewish equivalent of hosting a church bingo night.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: Because, in fact, her tits aren't that great. I mean, they're too big for her body.

jokes.text: Artie interjects about Hank's schedule: 'By things... by things, he means crying, by the way.'
jokes.setup: Hank says he would have to 'move some things around' to make Sajak's meeting.
jokes.punchline: Artie translates: those 'things' are crying.
jokes.explanation: Five-word gut-punch. The line perfectly summarizes Hank's entire emotional state this episode — the banana liqueur all-nighter, the fire extinguisher contemplation, the career desperation — condensed to 'he means crying.' Artie as brutal truth-teller in the most economical possible form. This line would be remembered by fans.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I'm this close to hitting you.

jokes.text: Larry, on air: 'For those of you who are watching tonight, the unemployment line starts right to the right of Pat.' — No flipping.
jokes.setup: Hank has just publicly pitched himself for Sajak's game show on Larry's own show.
jokes.punchline: Larry openly acknowledges on-air that his own people are job-hunting by pointing out where the unemployment line is. 'No flipping' follows.
jokes.explanation: Larry using the show's platform to make a bitter joke about his own staff's defection is quintessential Larry Sanders — the private anxiety leaking into the professional performance. The 'No flipping' punctuation gains extra irony here as the show's ending approaches.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: That's down near San diego.
No.
Missouri.

jokes.text: Donny and Marie Osmond bicker on the phone with Artie about producing their show — Marie keeps interrupting and Donny yells at her.
jokes.setup: Artie receives a call from Donny and Marie Osmond pitching him to produce their show.
jokes.punchline: Within seconds, Donny is screaming 'Marie, be quiet! Shut up, will ya!' while pitching 'the daytime spirit' — the chaos undermining the pitch.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the contrast between Donny and Marie's wholesome brand and Donny immediately snapping at his sister during a professional pitch call. 'That's the daytime spirit' is a nice ironic button. Celebrity self-mockery works here.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: 2 million fucking dollars?

jokes.text: Hank is auditioning to host a game show. Bob Eubanks is running it. Hank calls the contestant 'Merv' — then 'Jim' — instead of the correct name 'Jeff.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to host the game show professionally.
jokes.punchline: He gets the contestant's name wrong twice — first calling him 'Merv' (another game show host), then 'Jim' — suggesting Hank's frame of reference is entirely made up of TV personalities.
jokes.explanation: Hank calling the contestant 'Merv' first — another game show host — is a revealing detail. His mind goes to show business figures even when confronted with real people. Then 'Jim' when corrected shows he's not even listening. Good character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What about, uh, big Jew jamboree?

jokes.text: The game show question: name the Emma Lazarus poem engraved on the Statue of Liberty. Nobody knows it. Jeff — repeatedly called Jim by Hank — buzzes in with 'Colossus.'
jokes.setup: Hank is hosting the game show. A relatively simple general knowledge question is posed.
jokes.punchline: Jeff answers 'Colossus' — close but wrong (it's 'The New Colossus'). Hank's response to being called Jim again: 'I got it. Fuck me. Sorry.'
jokes.explanation: The accumulating chaos of the game show test — wrong name, wrong answer, Hank's exasperated 'Fuck me, sorry' — is well-constructed cringe. Not the strongest individual moment but contributes to the sequence.

jokes.text: After Jeff gets 'Colossus' wrong, Hank tells him: 'So I guess you should worry a little less about your name and a little more about these, uh... these questions.'
jokes.setup: Jeff correctly corrected Hank for calling him Jim. Jeff then got the answer wrong.
jokes.punchline: Hank turns Jeff's legitimate complaint against him by using his wrong answer as a weapon — displaying precisely the petty vindictiveness of a bad game show host.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Hank moment — he weaponizes Jeff's incorrect answer to win a petty argument about the name mix-up, demonstrating exactly why he cannot host a game show. The phrasing is controlled and almost articulate, which makes the pettiness funnier. Justified 8+ score: it's a precise character revelation delivered with comic craft.

jokes.text: Hank to female contestant Debbie, who has failed to answer: 'Not to worry, Debbie — with a body like yours, you don't have to be smart.'
jokes.setup: Debbie has failed to answer the question about the president who dedicated the Statue of Liberty.
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'consolation' is a sexually harassing comment delivered with game-show-host warmth, as if it's a compliment.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the sincere delivery — Hank genuinely thinks he's being kind. The cringe is maximal because the audition tape is rolling. The punchline is not the line itself but everything after: this tanks his game show career in real time.

jokes.text: After being dropped from the game show for sexual harassment: 'I paid a compliment to her on her body. I mean, is that a crime? I mean, I'm being kind. I'm just being generous. Because, in fact, her tits aren't that great. I mean, they're too big for her body.'
jokes.setup: Hank is defending himself against the sexual harassment complaint.
jokes.punchline: His defense of his 'generosity' collapses instantly when he clarifies that he actually doesn't even think her body is that good — making the harassment worse AND revealing his self-delusion simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Superb escalation — Hank's defense of being 'generous' and 'kind' immediately undermined by revealing he didn't even really mean the compliment. 'Because, in fact, her tits aren't that great' is the pivot that makes the joke. The logic is airtight in its absurdity: he harassed her AND the harassment was insincere. This is the episode's best sustained character comedy moment — could be the Hank version of the vasectomy speech anchor.

jokes.text: Hank continues: 'I paid a compliment to her on her body. Is that a crime? I'm being kind. I'm just being generous. Because, in fact, her tits aren't that great. I mean, they're too big for her body.'
jokes.setup: Hank defends his sexual harassment as generosity
jokes.punchline: His 'defense' doubles down — revealing that his 'compliment' was insincere because he actually doesn't even like her body ('too big for her body')
jokes.explanation: The escalation makes this land harder than the initial line. Hank's 'defense' accidentally reveals that his compliment was a lie — he doesn't even think she's attractive. This self-undermining logic (defending a compliment by revealing it was insincere) is brilliant character work. Tambor's reading is crucial here. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Someone attempts to motivate Hank: 'You have, uh, first of all, a huge talent and a fantastic voice and a lot of fans out there who love you, Hank Kingsley.' — long pause — 'Yeah. You got charm and you got personality. Your future's out there. All you have to do is reach out, grab on, and hang on for the ride.'
jokes.setup: Artie tries to motivate a despondent Hank.
jokes.punchline: The motivational speech is so hollow and generic that the pause between the first attempt and the second attempt says everything — even Artie can't quite commit to it.
jokes.explanation: The irony is that the famously brutal Artie is reduced to inspirational-poster platitudes. The implied pauses and the generic language undercut themselves. Not the episode's strongest moment but serves the character arc.

jokes.text: Hank's response to Artie's motivational speech: 'I'm this close to hitting you.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just delivered a sincere (if hollow) motivational speech to cheer Hank up.
jokes.punchline: Hank's genuine reaction to kindness is to threaten violence.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. The line is six words and communicates everything about the Hank-Artie relationship and Hank's emotional state. The violence threat as a response to kindness is both darkly funny and character-true. High quotability — this line leaves the episode with you. Justified 8+ score.

jokes.text: Hank to Artie mid-pep-talk: 'I'm this close to hitting you.'
jokes.setup: Artie is delivering an encouraging speech about Hank's future and talent, building to a motivational crescendo.
jokes.punchline: Hank's flat, intimate threat of violence — delivered at the moment of peak encouragement — is the perfect anti-motivational response.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. Six words that do everything: they reject the pep talk completely, they reveal the depth of Hank's despair (he's so far gone that kindness makes him violent), and they're unexpectedly funny because the threat is phrased with the restraint of a man who is barely holding it together. The economy is near-perfect. 'This close' implies measurement — Hank has calculated the distance between himself and assault. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quotability and economy. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: Andy Williams appears. Hank asks where he's been. Williams says he built a theater in Branson, Missouri. Hank: 'Oh, sure. That's down near San Diego.'
jokes.setup: Andy Williams mentions he built a theater in Branson, Missouri.
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately, confidently, and completely incorrectly locates Branson near San Diego — confusing Missouri with California.
jokes.explanation: Hank's geographic idiocy is delivered with total confidence — he doesn't frame it as a question. The specific error (confusing two states with nothing in common) reveals the California-bubble obliviousness of the Hollywood insider. Williams' implied reaction is the bonus.

jokes.text: Andy Williams reveals his Branson theater does over 6 million tourists a year and 2 shows a day, packed every night. Hank: '2 million fucking dollars? Good for you. Why not?'
jokes.setup: Andy Williams describes his wildly successful Branson theater business.
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'Why not?' is the perfect dismissive Hollywood response to success happening outside the industry bubble — simultaneously impressed and condescending.
jokes.explanation: The 'Why not?' after learning the scale of Williams' success is the joke — it's faint praise bordering on dismissal, completely inappropriate to the revelation of $2 million in November alone. Hank cannot process success that exists outside his frame of reference.

jokes.text: Larry asks about the money: '2 million fucking dollars? Good for you. Why not?'
jokes.setup: Andy has revealed he made over $2 million in November alone from Branson
jokes.punchline: Larry's expletive-laden amazement followed by the philosophically accepting 'why not?' — a hint of professional existential crisis
jokes.explanation: 'Why not?' is the perfect existentially deflated response. It has the quality of someone who has just realized he's been wrong about everything. The profanity is uncharacteristic enough to signal genuine surprise.

jokes.text: Hank, inspired by Andy Williams, announces: 'I'm going to Branson. I'm opening up the Hank Kingsley Hey Now Music Hall. Or the Hey Now Opry. I'm still fucking around with that name.'
jokes.setup: Andy Williams has described his Branson success. Hank has been having a crisis about his future.
jokes.punchline: Hank's instantaneous pivot to 'I'm opening a venue in Branson' — named after his catchphrase — is both grandiose and completely plausible given his delusions.
jokes.explanation: The 'Hey Now Music Hall / Hey Now Opry' is a great joke — Hank's brand identity is so thin that his entire business plan is just his catchphrase. 'I'm still fucking around with that name' is a perfect button: he's already in planning mode. High character integration, high quotability.

jokes.text: Artie's response to the Branson announcement: 'What about, uh, big Jew jamboree?'
jokes.setup: Hank has been workshopping venue names: 'Hey Now Music Hall' or 'Hey Now Opry.'
jokes.punchline: Artie contributes 'Big Jew Jamboree' — which is both more honest about Hank's brand and darkly funnier than anything Hank has proposed.
jokes.explanation: Three words that are the episode's comedic apex. 'Big Jew Jamboree' works on multiple levels: it's Artie's deadpan contribution to a name-brainstorm he clearly finds absurd; it uses self-aware Jewish identity humor (Artie and Hank are both Jewish); the word 'Jamboree' is the perfect Branson-adjacent country corniness, so it actually makes sense as a venue name; and the shock of the phrase coming from Rip Torn's Artie is maximum. This is the episode's standout quotable moment.

jokes.text: Pat Sajak reacts to the Branson announcement — implied reaction beat — then: 'Pat Sajak. I just got a job working for Pat Sajak.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just declared he's moving to Branson and opening a venue.
jokes.punchline: Immediately after the grand announcement, the scene cuts to someone (apparently Hank) flatly stating 'I just got a job working for Pat Sajak' — as if the Branson plan has already collapsed or was always fantasy.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition — grand Branson declaration immediately deflated by the mundane reality of 'I work for Pat Sajak now' — is a classic Larry Sanders structural joke. The show cuts back to earth. The callback to the Sajak pitch lands as both a plot resolution and a joke about Hank's self-delusion cycles.

tmdb_overview: Larry's staff prepares for the end by secretly looking for new jobs.
